blogs.title: When Expert Testimony Collapses: The Fatal Flaw in Finesse Wireless' Infringement Case
blogs.description: This post analyzes the Federal Circuit's sharp critique of Dr. Wells' contradictory testimony regarding the '134 patent. It explores how the court applied the *Johns Hopkins* standard to overturn a jury verdict based on an expert who appeared to pivot mid-testimony without providing a coherent theory. The discussion focuses on the evidentiary threshold for substantial evidence when an expert's opinion relies on conflicting interpretations of technical diagrams, effectively highlighting the risks plaintiffs face when their expert witnesses lack consistency.

blogs.title: Beyond Claim Construction: How Prosecution History Failed to Save Scope in Finesse Wireless
blogs.description: While many cases turn on the dictionary definition of claim terms, this blog examines why arguments regarding prosecution history estoppel and surrender were insufficient in *Finesse Wireless*. We will dissect the court's reasoning that amending claims from 'two or three' to 'three' signals did not constitute a 'clear and unambiguous' disclaimer against using two input signals. The analysis contrasts this outcome with stricter applications of prosecution history estoppel, offering insights into how Federal Circuit judges interpret amendments intended to distinguish prior art versus those viewed as mere clarification.

blogs.title: The Gap Between Theory and Reality: Reversing Infringement Due to Missing Multiplication Evidence
blogs.description: This article focuses on the evidentiary gap identified in the '775 patent portion of the decision. Specifically, it analyzes why identifying three distinct mathematical operations in a technical manual was legally insufficient to prove infringement of a claim requiring seven specific multiplications. The post discusses the dangers of extrapolating from partial data (three operations) to full claim coverage (seven operations) without direct evidence linking them, setting a precedent for how courts scrutinize technical mapping between accused devices and complex algorithmic claims.
